v.why: At very large learning rates wider layers amplify the effective function-space step and push training further past the divergence cliff.
With a fixed epoch budget, larger batches mean fewer updates, which compounds with tiny step sizes into severe undertraining.
Larger batches reduce gradient noise that otherwise destabilises training at high learning rates.
Deeper nets have a sharper stability cliff so a one-step learning-rate increase more often causes divergence.
Large batches give few updates per epoch, so a larger learning rate compensates and reduces undertraining.
Tiny batches produce very noisy updates, so lowering the learning rate stabilises training while many updates per epoch still allow convergence.
Very wide nets already have ample capacity, so extra depth mostly adds optimization difficulty and overfitting.
At very small learning rates the net is badly undertrained in 243 epochs, so a larger step directly improves fitting.
Already-large learning rates sit at or beyond the divergence edge, so going larger collapses accuracy.
Smaller batches give many more updates per epoch, which relieves undertraining when each step is tiny.
Smaller batches add gradient noise and more large-step updates, which pushes high-learning-rate training into instability.
Stacking more layers compounds large updates and makes high-learning-rate training more likely to diverge.
With tiny learning rates, more layers give more parameters moving per Adam step and so faster effective progress.
Under Adam each weight moves a fixed amount, so wider layers change the function more per step and ease undertraining at low learning rates.
With few updates from large batches, wider nets fit faster per step and so reduce undertraining.
Deeper nets amplify the noise of tiny-batch gradients, making training less stable.
Penalties near 0.1 to 1 start to dominate the loss and shrink weights enough to cause underfitting.
A single hidden layer gets its capacity only from width, so widening helps more than when depth already supplies capacity.
Going from already-large batches to the maximum cuts the number of updates further and increases undertraining.
Narrow nets have little spare capacity, so stronger L2 shrinkage pushes them into underfitting.

I kept 7 of the colleague's 20 hypotheses and replaced the other 13. The kept ones are the large, mechanistic interactions between learning rate, batch size and update count. The dropped ones were small-effect or sign-ambiguous: alpha interactions, and width or depth interactions with weak mechanisms. Most of those would not stay consistent across all three datasets.

I replaced the dropped ones with hypotheses built on the same strong effects:
- **Low learning rate:** it undertrains within 243 epochs, so anything that adds updates or capacity helps.
- **High learning rate:** it destabilises training, so anything that adds depth, noise or step amplification hurts.
- **Alpha:** it only matters in the extreme high band.
